story_report.summary: Hurricane Polo reached Category 5 strength off Mexico’s Pacific coast, with peak sustained winds exceeding 157 mph, before weakening to Category 4. At 3 a.m. CST on Sept. 23, the National Hurricane Center reported 155 mph winds and said the storm’s outer rainbands were beginning to reach southwestern Mexico. A tropical-storm warning was in effect from Tecpan de Galeana to Punta San Telmo, as authorities closed ports in Guerrero and Michoacán and suspended classes in some areas.

sections.heading: Polo’s Rapid Intensification
sections.body: Polo strengthened from a 40 mph tropical storm at 9 p.m. CST on Sept. 20 to maximum sustained winds near 180 mph by 1 p.m. CST on Sept. 22, according to NOAA Hurricane Hunter observations. Colorado State University atmospheric scientist Philip Klotzbach told AP that El Niño-linked warmer Pacific water and wind patterns created conditions that can allow hurricanes to intensify very rapidly. NHC analysts attributed the subsequent decline from Category 5 intensity to an eyewall replacement cycle observed in aircraft and satellite data.

sections.heading: Southwestern Mexico Faces Flood Threat
sections.body: The NHC forecast heavy rainfall through Thursday that could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in steep terrain. Mexico’s navy closed ports in Guerrero and Michoacán, while the U.S. Embassy advised people to avoid beaches and water and to follow Mexican authorities’ warnings. The coastal hazard remained despite forecasts taking Polo’s center farther offshore.

sections.heading: Polo Forecast to Move Offshore
sections.body: The NHC expected Polo to turn northwest and then west-northwest over the following days, moving its center farther from Mexico’s coast. Its Sept. 23 forecast kept winds near 155 mph through early Sept. 24, followed by gradual weakening to 140 mph by Sept. 26 and 105 mph by Sept. 28. President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts had indicated the storm was not likely to make landfall, according to AP reporting.

unresolved.text: The severity and location of coastal impacts remain dependent on Polo’s precise track, speed, rain-band placement and wind-field size; intensity may also fluctuate as inner-core changes and eyewall replacements continue.

stories.title: ICC Finds Former CAR Militia Commander Guilty of Crimes Against Humanity
stories.summary: The International Criminal Court has found Mahamat Said Abdel Kani, a former militia commander in the Central African Republic, guilty of crimes against humanity. He was determined to have overseen torture and abuse of prisoners at a detention facility in Bangui. The court's ruling highlights the brutal tactics employed during his leadership of a feared prison unit.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this conviction matter for CAR?
explore_lenses.title: It reaches the Séléka side of the conflict
explore_lenses.summary: The verdict is significant because the ICC’s CAR II investigation covers alleged crimes by groups linked to both the predominantly Muslim Séléka coalition and the mainly Christian anti-Balaka militias. Reuters reports that Said is the first Séléka member convicted by the court, extending individual accountability beyond the anti-Balaka cases.

claims.text: The CAR’s transitional authorities referred alleged crimes committed since August 1, 2012 to the ICC in May 2014; the ICC’s investigation has focused on alleged crimes by groups linked to both Séléka and anti-Balaka forces.
Reuters reports that Said is the first Séléka member convicted by the ICC, after the court convicted two anti-Balaka leaders.
The ruling concerns one defendant and does not amount to a judicial finding about responsibility for all violence during CAR’s conflict.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a verdict?
explore_lenses.title: A long ICC process followed the 2013 abuses
explore_lenses.summary: The case moved from a sealed 2019 arrest warrant to Said’s surrender in 2021, a trial beginning in 2022, and closing arguments in late 2025. The defense denied the charges, while judges ultimately found the prosecution had proved four crimes against humanity.

claims.text: The ICC issued Said’s arrest warrant under seal on January 7, 2019; he was surrendered to the court on January 24, 2021, and his trial opened on September 26, 2022.
The prosecution concluded its evidence in November 2024 after calling 58 witnesses; the defense concluded its case on September 2, 2025, and closing statements were heard on November 25-26, 2025.
Said denied all charges; his defense previously characterized the prosecution’s account as biased and incomplete.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the guilty verdict?
explore_lenses.title: Sentencing and a possible appeal remain
explore_lenses.summary: The conviction does not yet establish Said’s prison term. A separate ICC hearing is expected to determine sentence, and the Rome Statute provides routes to appeal convictions and sentences.

claims.text: Judges convicted Said on four crimes-against-humanity counts, including persecution and torture, while dismissing several war-crimes charges after finding the armed conflict had ended when some alleged conduct occurred.
A separate hearing will determine Said’s sentence.
The Rome Statute permits the convicted person or prosecutor to appeal a conviction or sentence on specified grounds, so the verdict may not be final until appeal rights are resolved or expire.

story_report.summary: International Criminal Court judges convicted former Central African Republic militia commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of four counts of crimes against humanity, including persecution and torture, for overseeing the torture and abuse of prisoners at a detention facility in the country. The court dismissed several war-crimes charges after finding that the armed conflict had ended when some alleged conduct occurred. A separate hearing will determine his sentence; no date or proposed penalty had been reported as of Sept. 23, 2026.

sections.heading: CAR Referral and ICC Investigation
sections.body: CAR’s transitional authorities referred alleged crimes committed from Aug. 1, 2012, to the ICC in May 2014. The court’s investigation has examined alleged crimes by groups linked to both the Séléka and anti-Balaka forces. Reuters reported that Said is the first Séléka member convicted by the ICC, following convictions of two anti-Balaka leaders.

sections.heading: Said Defense and Trial Timeline
sections.body: The ICC issued Said’s arrest warrant under seal in January 2019, and he was surrendered to the court in January 2021. His trial began in September 2022; prosecutors finished presenting evidence in November 2024 after calling 58 witnesses, while the defense concluded in September 2025 and closing statements followed in November. Said denied all charges, and his defense had described the prosecution’s account as biased and incomplete.

sections.heading: Said Sentencing and Appeal Rights
sections.body: Sentencing proceedings are the likely next substantive public stage because the court deferred punishment to a separate hearing. Under the Rome Statute, either the convicted person or the prosecutor may appeal a conviction or sentence on specified grounds. The verdict therefore may not become final until appeal rights are resolved or expire.

stories.title: Iran's President Responds to Trump's Threat at UN General Assembly
stories.summary: In a speech at the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian declared that Iran would not surrender following U.S. President Donald Trump's threat to 'annihilate' the Islamic Republic. Pezeshkian characterized Iran as a victim of U.S. terrorism, showcasing images of Iranian civilians affected by military actions. His address came amid ongoing conflict between Iran and the U.S. and Israel.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The “Iran War” refers to the 2026 armed conflict between the United States and Iran, involving Israeli strikes and wider regional attacks, alongside recurring diplomatic efforts to halt hostilities. It has centered in part on security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, making the conflict consequential for Gulf states and global energy markets.

facts.label: Start of major hostilities
facts.value: The UN Secretary-General said that the United States and Israel launched major strikes against Iran on February 28, 2026, followed by Iranian attacks affecting Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. In a March 10 letter to the Security Council, the United States said it had begun combat operations on February 28 and characterized them as self-defense.

facts.label: Main parties and geography
facts.value: The core interstate conflict is between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, with Israel participating in the initial strikes and Gulf states affected by subsequent regional attacks. The Strait of Hormuz—between Iran and Oman and linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea—has been a central operational and diplomatic focus.

facts.label: Maritime and economic significance
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a major energy chokepoint: the U.S. Energy Information Administration has described it as the world’s most important oil-transit chokepoint because of the volumes of petroleum moving through it. UN reporting during the conflict said ship transits had fallen by more than 90% after the crisis escalated in late February 2026.

facts.label: Diplomatic track
facts.value: Ceasefire and negotiation efforts have accompanied the fighting. The UN welcomed a June 2026 U.S.-Iran peace arrangement calling for a permanent ceasefire, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further talks, while later UN briefings described the situation as fragile and noted renewed military exchanges in late June.

facts.label: Legal and U.S. constitutional framework
facts.value: Internationally, the UN Charter requires states to settle disputes peacefully and prohibits threats or uses of force inconsistent with the Charter; the law of the sea recognizes transit passage through straits used for international navigation. explore_lenses.label: What changed on the ground and at sea?
explore_lenses.title: Hormuz has become a central pressure point
explore_lenses.summary: The UN speeches took place as the war’s effects extended beyond Iran’s territory to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Pezeshkian paired his defiance with a warning that unequal access to the waterway and an expanded military presence would not produce peace.

claims.text: Pezeshkian told the General Assembly that the Strait of Hormuz had become a focal point of U.S.-Iran tensions and said Iran could not accept others benefiting from the route while it was denied shipping access.

Before the UN meetings, a senior Iranian official said Iran could reopen Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and ended its blockade of Iranian ports; this was a reported proposal, not an agreed arrangement.

The UN human-rights office said the wider hostilities had affected 12 other states and damaged homes, airports and energy infrastructure; it also reported civilian casualties in Iran and Iranian missile and drone attacks on states across the region.

explore_lenses.summary: Washington says its campaign is meant to stop Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon and to counter Iranian-backed violence. Tehran characterizes the February 28 U.S.-Israeli attack and subsequent strikes as unlawful aggression, foregrounding civilian casualties and alleged attacks on protected sites.

claims.text: The White House said Trump’s UN address framed Iran as a terrorism sponsor and said U.S. policy would not allow Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s UN representative has stated that the war began on February 28, 2026, with U.S.-Israeli attacks; this is Iran’s official characterization of the conflict and responsibility for it.

The UN human-rights office called for a prompt, impartial and thorough investigation of the strike on a Minab primary school, noting reports that girls were killed and injured. It did not in that statement assign legal responsibility for the attack.

Iran has submitted UN documents alleging that U.S. missile strikes destroyed the Minab school and killed more than 168 students, but those documents present Iran’s account and casualty figures rather than an independently adjudicated finding.

explore_lenses.title: Indirect contacts resumed, but no deal is public
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate diplomatic development was not a U.S.-Iran presidential meeting but mediated, indirect communication on the UN sidelines. Both sides signaled interest in diplomacy while retaining incompatible public positions and military threats.

claims.text: Reuters reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators at the UN—the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire collapsed in July.
Trump described the engagement as a productive meeting with Iranian mediators, while Reuters reported that neither side publicly described a change in its negotiating position.
Pezeshkian said Iran would not surrender but believed diplomacy could help end the conflict, while Trump’s UN address presented a deal as an alternative to further escalation.

The UN General Assembly’s general debate was scheduled to continue through September 26 and resume September 28, providing a continuing venue for bilateral and mediated contacts but not a confirmed peace-negotiation timetable.

story_report.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian used his address to the UN General Assembly to reject President Donald Trump’s threat to “annihilate” Iran. Pezeshkian said Iran would not surrender, described the country as a victim of U.S. terrorism and argued that diplomacy could help end the conflict. The competing public positions were aired as Iranian and U.S. representatives communicated through mediators at the UN, their first reported contacts since an interim ceasefire collapsed in July, although neither side publicly announced a change in its negotiating stance.

sections.heading: Hormuz Dispute and Regional Damage
sections.body: Pezeshkian said the Strait of Hormuz had become a focal point of tensions, arguing that Iran could not accept other countries benefiting from the route while it was denied shipping access. Before the UN meetings, a senior Iranian official proposed reopening the strait to Gulf shipping within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and ended its blockade of Iranian ports; the proposal was not an agreement. The UN human-rights office said the wider hostilities had affected 12 other states and damaged homes, airports and energy infrastructure, while causing civilian casualties in Iran and prompting Iranian missile and drone attacks across the region.

sections.heading: Washington and Tehran State Rival Accounts
sections.body: The White House said Trump’s UN address portrayed Iran as a sponsor of terrorism and maintained that U.S. policy would prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran’s UN representative has said the war began with U.S.-Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, 2026, an official Iranian characterization of responsibility for the conflict. Iran has also alleged in UN submissions that U.S. missile strikes destroyed a primary school in Minab and killed more than 168 students, while the UN human-rights office has called for a prompt, impartial investigation without assigning legal responsibility.

The General Assembly’s debate was scheduled to continue through Sept. 26 and resume on Sept. 28, leaving a venue for further contacts but no confirmed peace-negotiation timetable.

stories.title: Kyiv Struck by Russian Drones Ahead of Zelenskyy's UN Address
stories.summary: On Wednesday, Kyiv was targeted by Russian drone strikes, resulting in two fatalities and 23 injuries. The attacks occurred just hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly. The strikes hit various locations, including railway infrastructure and fuel stations, amid ongoing tensions in the region.

timeline_highlights.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has ordered protective measures for the country's critical infrastructure and defense industry in response to escalating Russian hybrid attacks. Macron emphasized that the hybrid threat from Moscow has intensified in recent weeks, necessitating immediate action.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next for the Golan dispute?
explore_lenses.title: Negotiations and ceasefire monitoring remain central
explore_lenses.summary: A UN address does not create a territorial settlement. The established practical framework is the 1974 Israel-Syria disengagement agreement, monitored by UNDOF; any sovereignty settlement would require political agreement between the parties.

claims.text: Security Council Resolution 350 welcomed the 1974 Israel-Syria disengagement agreement and created the UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) to supervise it.
UNDOF’s stated role is to maintain the ceasefire and supervise the disengagement agreement between Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan.

UNDOF said in December 2024 that it had observed Israeli military movements in the area of separation and regarded them as violations of the 1974 agreement, while urging all parties to cease military activity there.

story_report.summary: Harvey Weinstein was sentenced in New York to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting Miriam Haley in 2006, following a retrial after his earlier New York judgment was overturned. The sentence applies to the conviction involving Haley and follows a legal process that has included multiple proceedings over allegations involving other women. It imposes a new prison term on the first-degree criminal-sex-act conviction returned by a Manhattan jury in 2025.

sections.heading: New York Retrial Followed Reversal
sections.body: Weinstein’s original 2020 New York judgment imposed a 23-year sentence on convictions involving Haley and Jessica Mann. In April 2024, New York’s highest court reversed that judgment and ordered a new trial, finding that the first trial had improperly admitted testimony concerning uncharged alleged acts and permitted potentially prejudicial cross-examination. At the retrial, a Manhattan jury convicted Weinstein on June 11, 2025, of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley.

sections.heading: Haley Conviction Defines New Sentence
sections.body: The 15-year term concerns the Haley conviction rather than all allegations raised during Weinstein’s New York cases. The count carried a maximum possible sentence of 25 years, and prosecutors had sought 20 years before sentencing. In the 2025 retrial, the jury acquitted Weinstein on a separate allegation and did not reach a verdict on the Mann rape count; after a later mistrial on that count, prosecutors ultimately dropped the rape charge rather than try it a fourth time.

sections.heading: Weinstein Challenges New York Proceedings
sections.body: Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg described the 2025 verdict as accountability for Haley and thanked her for testifying again. Weinstein has denied sexually assaulting or raping anyone, while his defense has argued that the proceedings were unfair. His lawyers have also challenged the 2025 New York conviction by alleging juror intimidation and outside bias; those assertions are defense arguments, not findings of misconduct.

unresolved.text: It remains unresolved whether New York appellate litigation will alter Weinstein’s new conviction or 15-year sentence.

The time Weinstein will ultimately remain incarcerated depends on sentence-credit calculations and continuing litigation in New York and California. California’s appellate court affirmed his 2022 Los Angeles convictions but vacated the 16-year sentence for resentencing, and he has petitioned the California Supreme Court for review.

event_overview.title: About Congressional Redistricting
event_overview.subject: Congressional Redistricting
event_overview.summary: Congressional redistricting is the process of setting the boundaries for Missouri’s eight U.S. House districts. This dispute concerns a mid-decade map enacted as House Bill 1 in 2025, a voter referendum challenging that law, and overlapping state and federal court proceedings over which map may govern the 2026 general election.

facts.label: Representation
facts.value: Missouri is divided into eight congressional districts for elections to the U.S. House of Representatives.

facts.label: Competing maps
facts.value: The earlier congressional plan was enacted in 2022; House Bill 1, enacted during the Missouri General Assembly’s 2025 Second Extraordinary Session, established a replacement set of congressional-district boundaries.

facts.label: Referendum process
facts.value: Missouri’s constitution permits a referendum on most laws through petitions signed by 5% of legal voters in each of two-thirds of the state’s congressional districts, with petitions due within 90 days after final adjournment of the session that passed the bill.

facts.label: State-court ruling
facts.value: On September 3, 2026, the Supreme Court of Missouri held that the referendum petition against HB 1 was legal, sufficient, and timely; it ruled that HB 1 would not take effect unless approved by voters and that the 2022 districts remained in force for the November 2026 general election.

facts.label: Federal litigation
facts.value: The related federal case concerns whether federal constitutional provisions require use of the 2025 map despite the state referendum ruling. On September 10, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed a September 8 federal district-court order while appellate proceedings continued.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the September 2026 court actions affecting which congressional map could be used for the general election, not Missouri’s full redistricting history or every related lawsuit and election-administration step.
